stem: A silver job receives one meter reading per row, and the device often sends NULL when a sensor skips a measurement. Analysts need every row to carry the most recent non-NULL `temp` of the same `device_id` at or before its `ts`. Which expression does this without a self-join?

choices.text: `last(temp, true) OVER (PARTITION BY device_id ORDER BY ts ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)`
`lag(temp, 1) OVER (PARTITION BY device_id ORDER BY ts)`, which returns the value of the previous row even when it is NULL
`max(temp) OVER (PARTITION BY device_id ORDER BY ts ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)` to carry the highest earlier value
`first_value(temp, true) OVER (PARTITION BY device_id ORDER BY ts ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)` to read the earliest non-NULL value

stem: A gold job needs one row per `sensor_id` that holds the three readings with the latest `ts` as an array. The team wants a single `GROUP BY sensor_id` aggregate, with no window function and no self-join. Which expression does this?

choices.text: `max_by(reading, ts)`, which returns the `reading` values of the three rows with the largest `ts` as an array
`max_by(reading, ts, 3)`, which returns an array with the readings of the three rows with the largest `ts`
`collect_list(reading)`, which returns the readings as an array sorted by `ts` from the newest to the oldest
`first(reading, 3)`, which returns the first three `reading` values of each group in arrival order

stem: A report uses `GROUP BY ROLLUP(region, channel)` and shows a row with `region = 'EU'` and `channel = NULL`. Some analysts read it as "EU sales with no channel recorded", but the source also contains genuine NULL channels. How should the query tell the subtotal row from real NULL data?

choices.text: Add `DISTINCT` to the select list, which removes the subtotal rows that repeat a region and leaves only the genuine NULL channels
Wrap `channel` in `coalesce(channel, 'ALL')`, which returns the label only for subtotal rows and never for source NULLs
Select `grouping(channel)` next to the columns; it is 1 for rows where `channel` was aggregated away and 0 for real values, including NULL
Replace `ROLLUP` with `GROUP BY region, channel` and add the totals later in a separate union with the same two columns

stem: Events were stored as JSON strings and queried with `payload:Customer_ID`. After the table was migrated to a VARIANT column built with `parse_json`, the same query returns NULL for every row, while the data still contains the key `customer_id`. What explains this?

choices.text: `parse_json` stores keys in alphabetical order and the engine matches by position, so a renamed key cannot be found
`parse_json` renames keys to lower case on conversion, so the query needs the stored key written in upper case instead
The `:` operator works only on STRING columns, so the query needs `get_json_object` over the column
VARIANT paths are case-sensitive, so `Customer_ID` and `customer_id` are different fields and the exact key is required

stem: A VARIANT column `raw` contains the key `zip.code`. The query `SELECT raw:`zip.code` FROM addresses` returns NULL for every row, although the key is present with values. Which change returns the values?

choices.text: Write `raw:['zip.code']`, because bracket notation escapes periods and square brackets in field names
Wrap the whole column in `to_json(raw)` and apply the colon operator to the resulting string
Cast the column first with `raw::string`, since VARIANT paths cannot contain periods before a cast
Write `raw:zip.code`, because the VARIANT operator takes a dotted name as one field key

stem: A VARIANT column `payload` holds an order with an array `items` of objects such as `{"sku":"A1","qty":2}`. A fact table needs one row per item with `sku` and `qty` as typed columns. Which query builds it?

choices.text: `SELECT o.id, explode(o.payload:items) FROM orders o`, because the generic function is the only one that unpacks arrays
`SELECT o.id, payload:items[*].sku FROM orders o`, which expands all array elements into separate rows
`SELECT o.id, i.value:sku::string AS sku, i.value:qty::int AS qty FROM orders o, LATERAL variant_explode(o.payload:items) i`
`SELECT o.id, payload:items:sku::string FROM orders o GROUP BY o.id`, which flattens the array while grouping by order

stem: A bronze table stores webhook bodies from 30 partners as VARIANT. Before promoting stable fields into typed silver columns, the team wants one summary of the combined structure and types seen across the whole column, including fields that appear only in some rows. Which function fits?

choices.text: `schema_of_json_agg(payload)`, which accepts VARIANT input and merges the field types of every row
`schema_of_variant(payload)` applied to the first row only, since one row always holds all possible fields
`payload::string` followed by a `DESCRIBE` of the table, because the metadata lists the nested fields of VARIANT columns
`schema_of_variant_agg(payload)`, which merges the schemas of all rows and falls back to VARIANT for conflicting types

stem: A nightly ingest runs `SELECT parse_json(body) AS v FROM bronze_raw`. One partner occasionally sends truncated JSON and the whole job fails. Bad rows must be kept for inspection, and good rows must flow. What is the best design?

choices.text: Keep `parse_json` and set `failOnError => false` on the call so that the failed rows come back as error messages for review
Use `try_parse_json(body)`, which returns NULL on invalid JSON, and route NULL results with non-NULL input to a rejects table
Cast with `body::variant`, which silently converts malformed JSON text to a VARIANT string value
Wrap the call in `ai_query` to repair broken JSON before parsing, so that no row ever fails

stem: A VARIANT column `v` holds events like `{"id":1,"coupon":null}` and `{"id":2}`. A data quality check must count events where the key `coupon` is present with an explicit JSON null, separately from events without the key. Which predicates separate the two cases?

choices.text: `try_variant_get(v, '$.coupon', 'string') IS NULL` is true only for the explicit null and false for a key that is missing
`v:coupon = 'null'` is true for the explicit null, while a missing key returns the string `'missing'`
`v:coupon IS NULL` is true for both cases, so the cases cannot be told apart in SQL at all
`is_variant_null(v:coupon)` is true when the key holds an explicit null, while `v:coupon IS NULL` is true when the key is missing

stem: A team wants to enable VARIANT on an existing Delta table that is also read by an external engine using a Delta Lake reader library. What must the team consider before running `ALTER TABLE ... SET TBLPROPERTIES('delta.feature.variantType' = 'supported')`?

choices.text: Enabling it upgrades the table writer protocol, which can break external Delta clients without support for it
The feature can be enabled only when the table is created, so an existing table must be recreated from scratch
VARIANT requires converting the table to Iceberg v2 first, because Delta tables cannot store any kind of semi-structured data type
The command rewrites all data files into a new layout, so the table is unavailable until the rewrite completes

stem: A compliance team must be able to prove the exact text of every webhook body received. The bronze table stores `body` as STRING and a derived column `v = parse_json(body)`. An engineer proposes to drop `body` and keep only `v`, converting back with `to_json(v)` when needed. What is the problem?

choices.text: VARIANT values are stored as compressed archives that cannot be read after 30 days, so the raw text must be kept
`parse_json` is not exactly reversible: whitespace, key order and trailing zeros are not preserved, so keep the raw text
`to_json` cannot convert a VARIANT value back to text, so the conversion is not available at all
The conversion only changes the data type, so the proposal is safe and the original text can be rebuilt byte for byte from the stored VARIANT value

stem: A batch enrichment job runs `SELECT id, ai_query('databricks-llama', 'Summarize: ' || text) AS summary FROM tickets` over 8 million rows. A few hundred rows hit endpoint errors, and the entire query fails and discards hours of work. The team wants the other rows to complete and the failures to be retried later. What should change?

choices.text: Wrap the call in `try_cast`, which turns any endpoint error into NULL before it can fail the query
Switch the table to a provisioned throughput endpoint, which never returns row-level errors
Add `failOnError => false`; each result becomes a struct with response and error message, so failed rows can be selected and retried later
Split the table into thousands of small queries run one after another, so that an endpoint error only hits a small part of the data

stem: A pipeline runs `ai_query` over 50 million documents once a day. An engineer proposes to chunk the table into 5,000-row slices in a Python loop and call the function per slice, to "protect the endpoint". What is the better design?

choices.text: Collect the documents to the driver and call the model serving REST API with a thread pool for full control
Use a provisioned throughput endpoint for the batch, because pay-per-token endpoints cannot serve batch queries from SQL
Keep the loop, but add a sleep between slices, because AI Functions cannot run in parallel on a cluster
Send the whole dataset in one query to a Databricks-hosted foundation model endpoint and let AI Functions parallelize and retry

stem: A pipeline uses `ai_query` to extract `vendor`, `total` and `due_date` from invoice text. The current prompt asks for JSON and a downstream `from_json` step fails on about 3% of rows because the model adds explanatory text. Which change makes the output reliably parseable?

choices.text: Lower the model temperature to zero in `modelParameters`, which guarantees that the model returns valid JSON every time
Add a second `ai_query` call that asks the model to check whether its first answer was valid JSON
Pass a `responseFormat` with a JSON schema or DDL schema, so the chat model must return output that follows it
Apply `regexp_extract` to remove all text before the first brace, which works for any model output

stem: A platform team wants analysts to run ready-made text classification and translation, while data engineers can also run custom prompts against chosen models in pipelines. How do the two kinds of AI Functions differ?

choices.text: Task-specific functions require the engineer to create a model serving endpoint first, while `ai_query` needs no endpoint
Task-specific functions such as `ai_translate` cover one task; `ai_query` is the general-purpose function for custom prompts and models
`ai_query` is limited to traditional ML endpoints, while task-specific functions are the only route to a large language model
Task-specific functions run only on classic SQL warehouses, while `ai_query` runs only on serverless compute and notebooks

stem: A governance team removed `EXECUTE` on the `system.ai` schema from all users and granted it back for only `ai_translate` and `ai_summarize`. Analysts can still run `ai_query` against a hosted foundation model. Why?

choices.text: These permissions do not govern `ai_query`, which calls a serving endpoint, so endpoint permissions control it
`ai_query` is exempt only for users with workspace admin rights, and the analysts are admins
The privilege change is cached for 24 hours, so `ai_query` is blocked only after the metastore has refreshed its privileges
Revoking `EXECUTE` on a schema affects only SQL warehouses, and analysts use notebooks on classic clusters

stem: Finance asks which jobs spend the most on LLM calls made with `ai_query` against Databricks-hosted foundation model endpoints. Where should the data engineer look?

choices.text: In the compute metrics of the job cluster, because the inference runs on the same cluster that submits the query
In `system.billing.usage` records with product `MODEL_SERVING` and offering type `BATCH_INFERENCE`, joined to job metadata
In `system.billing.usage` records with product `AI_FUNCTIONS`, since `ai_query` is always recorded under that product
Only in the Spark UI of each job, because AI Function costs are not stored in system tables

stem: An engineer wants to give each row its own output limit: `modelParameters => named_struct('max_tokens', t.limit_tokens)`, where `limit_tokens` is a column, and the query is rejected. What is the rule?

choices.text: Model parameters are ignored unless `failOnError` is set to false, so the engineer must enable it first
Model parameters are accepted only for custom model endpoints, and a hosted foundation model needs the limit in the prompt text
Model parameters must be constant values and cannot depend on row data, so use a fixed value or run separate queries per limit
The struct must be passed through `responseFormat`, which is the only argument that accepts column references

stem: A job must describe product photos stored as files in a Unity Catalog volume with a hosted vision model. The folder contains JPEG, PNG and TIFF files. Which approach fits the multimodal support of `ai_query`?

choices.text: Read with `read_files` as `binaryFile`, pass `files => content`, and convert TIFF files to JPEG or PNG first
Use `files => path`, because the parameter takes the file location and reads any format
Base64-encode every file in a UDF and concatenate it into the prompt, which works for all formats
Pass the file path strings in the prompt text, because the endpoint downloads the images from the Unity Catalog volume itself

stem: A streaming table receives trip records. Rows with a NULL pickup or dropoff zip must not reach the gold reports, but compliance requires keeping them for review with the reason. Which design in a Lakeflow pipeline meets both needs?

choices.text: A plain `expect` on one table, since invalid rows are automatically written to a separate quarantine table
`expect_or_drop` on the zip rules; the dropped count in the metrics is enough to review the cases
`expect_or_fail` on the zip rules, so that any invalid trip stops the whole update until someone fixes the source data
Add an `is_quarantined` flag in a table with `expect_all`, then expose valid and invalid rows as two views

stem: A triggered pipeline has a validation materialized view with `expect_or_fail("unique_pk", "num_entries = 1")` that checks the primary key of the `report` table. A violation is found, the validation flow fails, yet the downstream `report_export` table updated successfully with the duplicates. What explains this?

choices.text: Only that flow is rolled back in a triggered pipeline; a validation table does not gate other tables, which update on their own
Fail expectations apply only to streaming tables, so the materialized view only warned and recorded the violation metrics instead of failing
The pipeline needs a continuous mode to evaluate expectations, and a triggered update skips them
The failure is retried in the background, and `report_export` read the data before the retry finished

stem: A continuous pipeline contains a streaming table `payments_clean` with `expect_or_fail("positive_amount", "amount > 0")`, which feeds three downstream tables. One bad record arrives. What is the result, and what must the team do?

choices.text: The flow pauses for one minute and then resumes automatically with the bad record written to the target
Only the failing flow stops, while the three downstream tables keep updating from data already in `payments_clean`
The flow and its dependent flows stop and the pipeline reports why; the code must be fixed before restart
Only the bad record is skipped and the stream continues, and the team reviews the dropped count later

stem: An `expect_or_fail("temperature_in_valid_range", "temperature BETWEEN -50 AND 60")` stops an update. The engineer must find which input record broke it. Where is that information, and which statement about metrics is true?

choices.text: The event log never has information for failures, so the engineer must rerun the pipeline with debug logging
The failing record is written to a quarantine table automatically, and the update is partly committed
Only the Data quality tab lists the failing record, and it shows a count of failed records for fail actions
The failure message names the expectation and shows the records in many queries; fail actions record no metrics

stem: A data platform team maintains the same 8 data quality rules for 25 Python datasets in several pipelines. Rules change monthly, and auditors want rule changes recorded without editing pipeline code. What is the recommended structure?

choices.text: Define the rules in a SQL file and read them with a dynamic expectation clause, which SQL expectations support
Keep the rules in a tagged Delta table, load them into a dictionary and pass it to `expect_all_or_drop`
Copy the rule strings into each dataset decorator, so that every pipeline stays self-contained and reviewable alone
Set the rules as pipeline configuration parameters and expect the engine to apply them to all datasets automatically

stem: A silver streaming table must keep every record for a new data source while analysts learn how bad the data is. After a month the team wants to start removing the invalid records. How should the actions be sequenced?

choices.text: Start with plain `expect` to keep rows and collect metrics, then switch stable rules to `expect_or_drop`
Start with `expect_or_drop` and rebuild dropped rows from the event log whenever analysts need them
Start with `expect_or_fail` so that bad data never lands in the table, then relax to `drop` once the data is clean
Start without expectations and add them only at the gold layer, where invalid rows cannot affect metrics

stem: An engineer defines a streaming table in a standalone pipeline created in Databricks SQL with `CONSTRAINT valid_amount EXPECT (amount > 0) ON VIOLATION DROP ROW`, and looks for the Data quality tab in the pipeline UI. The tab is missing. Where can the expectation metrics be read?

choices.text: In the query history of the SQL warehouse, which stores the number of dropped rows per statement
By querying the pipeline event log, since the Data quality tab is unavailable for standalone SQL pipelines
Only in the table history of the target table, where the dropped count is shown as an operation metric of each write
Nowhere, because expectations on Databricks SQL streaming tables do not record any metrics at all

stem: A pipeline uses an AUTO CDC FROM SNAPSHOT flow to maintain a dimension from periodic snapshots. The team adds an expectation to the flow's target definition and gets no enforcement and no metrics. What is the right way to validate the dimension?

choices.text: Add the expectation as a SQL comment, which Lakeflow Pipelines read as a data quality rule
Increase the snapshot frequency, because expectations evaluate only when two snapshots differ by at least one changed row
Put the expectation on a downstream dataset that reads the dimension, since this flow does not support expectations
Convert the flow to a standard append flow, which is the only flow type that can write the dimension

stem: A team writes its pipelines in SQL and wants to apply one shared set of 10 rules with a single drop action to 30 tables, the way Python authors use `expect_all_or_drop` with a dictionary. What is true for SQL datasets?

choices.text: SQL expectations cannot drop rows, so a shared drop action must be implemented in a Python dataset that reads the SQL output
SQL has an `EXPECT ALL` clause that reads a rules table by tag, which is the SQL equivalent of the Python dictionary helper
SQL supports only one expectation per dataset, so the 10 rules must be combined into a single boolean expression joined with `AND`
Grouping rules with a collective action is Python only; in SQL each rule is its own `CONSTRAINT ... EXPECT ... ON VIOLATION DROP ROW` clause

stem: A streaming table in a pipeline has `expect_or_drop` rules. An engineer sums the expectation counts from `flow_progress` event log rows whose status is `COMPLETED` and gets no counts for some updates, although rows were dropped. Which change finds the counts?

choices.text: Query the Delta history of the target table, where each streaming write stores the dropped-row count
Switch the rules to `expect_or_fail`, because fail actions record the complete expectation metrics in the final event of every update, even when the update itself fails
Run a full refresh of the table, which rewrites the metrics into the `COMPLETED` event of the update
Also read the `flow_progress` events with status `RUNNING`, because for some flows the metrics are reported per micro-batch there

stem: A nightly Lakeflow Jobs job has a `For each` task that runs a child notebook for 400 tables, and the run ends as Failed. The engineer must find the iterations that failed and read their outputs without scrolling through all 400. What does the run view offer for this?

choices.text: The Finished runs count graph shows each failed iteration as a separate run, and filtering it by error code opens that iteration directly
The Timeline view groups the iterations by outcome, because it lists failed iterations first and links each one to its notebook output
The run details of the `For each` task present the iterations as a table, and an "Only failed iterations" toggle lists just the failures so each can be opened
The job-level matrix gives every iteration of the `For each` task its own cell in the Tasks row, with the failed cells sorted to the left

stem: Auditors require the rendered output of every run of a nightly notebook job to be available for six months. The engineer sees that the Jobs UI keeps the run history for 60 days. What should the engineer do to meet the requirement?

choices.text: Export the notebook run results to HTML before the runs expire and store the files outside the run history, because expired runs and their outputs are not kept
Raise the retention of the job to 180 days in its advanced settings, because the 60-day history is only the default value of a per-job setting
Configure an expected completion time for the job, because runs that exceed their expected duration are exempt from the 60-day cleanup
Mark the job as a favorite in the Jobs & Pipelines list, because runs of favorite jobs are excluded from the 60-day cleanup

stem: A managed Delta table is maintained by a nightly job that runs `OPTIMIZE sales ZORDER BY (customer_id)`. The team enables predictive optimization on the table and removes the job, expecting the Z-order on `customer_id` to stay current. Over the following weeks filters on `customer_id` get slower as new data arrives. What explains this, and what is the lasting fix?

choices.text: Predictive optimization is only an observer of the nightly job, so the job must be restored for any `OPTIMIZE` or `ZORDER` to run on the table
Predictive optimization runs `OPTIMIZE` without `ZORDER`, so new files are never Z-ordered; move the table to liquid clustering on `customer_id`, which predictive optimization maintains
Predictive optimization repeats the old `ZORDER BY` once a week, so the slowdown disappears at the next weekly run without any change
Predictive optimization applies `ZORDER` only to partition columns, so the table must first be partitioned by `customer_id` before the Z-order is kept current

stem: Finance asks where predictive optimization does its work and how it is billed, because the engineer was told that it is not charged to any team cluster. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: It runs inside the control plane at no compute cost, so Finance has no usage to attribute and nothing to review for these operations
It runs on a shared SQL warehouse chosen at the catalog level, so the cost is part of that warehouse's bill and its query history lists the operations
It runs on the driver of the cluster that last wrote the table, so the cost is part of that cluster's bill and the Spark UI lists the operations
It runs on serverless compute for jobs, so no cluster is sized by the team, and the account is billed through a serverless jobs SKU

stem: A team enables predictive optimization on a catalog whose tables hold 90 days of history for audits and sometimes need time travel of 30 days. Weeks later, queries with `VERSION AS OF` older than 8 days fail because files are gone. No one ran `VACUUM`. What should have been done, and what fixes the future behavior?

choices.text: Run `OPTIMIZE` more often so that old versions are compacted into the newest version, because compaction keeps the files needed for time travel
Set `delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration` to 30 days on the tables before relying on predictive optimization, because its `VACUUM` honors that property
Disable `VACUUM` in the predictive optimization settings for the catalog, because the operation list can be edited per operation type on every table
Increase the `delta.logRetentionDuration` only, because the log retention alone controls how long data files stay on storage after vacuum

stem: A team runs a non-Databricks Spark application that must read a Unity Catalog managed Delta table. An engineer proposes giving the application cloud credentials and pointing it at the table's storage path in the bucket. Which approach does Databricks support instead?

choices.text: Read the path directly, because the restriction on path access applies to Databricks Runtime clients and not to open-source clients
Copy the files to a second bucket every night, because managed tables expose their files to outside engines only through scheduled exports
Read the table through the Unity REST API, which vends temporary credentials scoped to the table and keeps Unity Catalog access control in force
Grant the application's role access to the managed storage location, because managed table files are a documented interface for direct reads

stem: An engineer drops several external Delta tables and several managed tables in the same catalog to cut costs, then notices that cloud storage cost fell only for some of them. Which statement explains the difference and the operational advantage of managed tables?

choices.text: Dropping a managed table makes Databricks delete its files after a recovery period, while files of an external table stay and must be deleted manually from storage
Dropping an external table deletes its files immediately, while files of a managed table stay until `VACUUM` is run with a zero-hour retention
Dropping a managed table leaves files in place permanently, because the catalog cannot delete data it does not own, whereas external table files expire with the metastore
Dropping either type deletes the files after the recovery period, so the difference comes from the clusters that were still caching old files

stem: A streaming job appends micro-batches of about 5 MB each to a liquid-clustered managed table. Over weeks the data skipping on the clustering keys degrades, although the table definition never changed. Predictive optimization is disabled for this table. What explains the degradation and what is the lowest-overhead fix?

choices.text: Liquid clustering clusters only data written by batch jobs, so streaming writers never produce clustered files; convert the sink to a partitioned table to restore skipping
Clustering on write only triggers when a transaction reaches a size threshold, so small batches stay unclustered; enable predictive optimization so incremental clustering runs
Streaming checkpoints block clustering metadata, so the stream must be restarted with a new checkpoint each week to rebuild the data layout
Clustering keys expire after a fixed number of commits, so the keys must be re-declared with `ALTER TABLE ... CLUSTER BY` every night by a scheduled job

stem: A 20 TB Delta table receives a nightly `MERGE` that updates about 0.1% of rows scattered across most files. The job rewrites a large share of the Parquet files and runs for hours, while the reading queries are already fast. Which change targets the write cost, and what does it add?

choices.text: Run `VACUUM` before every merge, so old files do not slow the file lookup; reads then apply a lower retention threshold
Turn on the disk cache on all workers, so the files rewritten by `MERGE` are served from local SSD; reads then pay only the first fetch
Enable deletion vectors, so changed rows are marked in metadata instead of rewriting files; reads apply them until compaction rewrites the files
Add more clustering keys with `CLUSTER BY`, so changed rows land in fewer files; reads then need no extra work because keys are free

stem: After a platform team enabled deletion vectors on a Delta table, a downstream analytics service that uses an older open-source Delta reader begins failing on reads of the table, while Databricks queries work. The team cannot upgrade that reader this quarter. What is the supported way to restore compatibility?

choices.text: Rewrite the table with `VACUUM` at zero retention, because vacuum removes the deletion vector files and resets the protocol
Set `spark.databricks.delta.reorg.purgeMode` to `rows` on the older reader, because that configuration makes the reader ignore protocol features
Delete the `_delta_log` entries that mention deletion vectors, because readers fail on protocol actions that are older than the table
Drop the deletion vectors table feature from the table, which removes the feature from the protocol so older clients can read it again

stem: A table with deletion vectors enabled feeds a Presto-compatible symlink manifest, and the `GENERATE symlink_format_manifest` step now fails. Writers keep running throughout the day. Which sequence resolves it?

choices.text: Run `REORG TABLE ... APPLY (PURGE)` with no concurrent writes, then generate the manifest; incremental generation stays unsupported
Disable the disk cache on the cluster, then rerun the generation, because cached deletion vectors cause manifest generation to fail
Run `OPTIMIZE ZORDER BY` on the table, then enable incremental manifest generation with the table property, which supports deletion vectors natively
Run `VACUUM` with the default retention, then run the generation; vacuum rewrites files with deletion vectors into clean files

stem: A Delta table in the team's own external storage (not Unity Catalog managed) is queried all day with filters on `tenant_id` and `event_date`; this access pattern has been stable for a year. The team wants better data skipping without partitioning. Which choice is correct?

choices.text: Use `CLUSTER BY AUTO`, because automatic liquid clustering selects keys for any Delta table, including external tables outside Unity Catalog management
Enable deletion vectors, because they store min and max values per file and improve data skipping on filtered columns
Set manual keys with `CLUSTER BY (tenant_id, event_date)`, because automatic key selection is only available for Unity Catalog managed tables
Enable predictive optimization on the table and leave the keys unset, because it chooses keys for external tables from query history

stem: A managed table uses explicit keys `CLUSTER BY (region)`. Analysts always filter on `region` but other filters have drifted over time. The team wants to keep `region` as a starting hint and let Databricks adapt further. Which statements do this?

choices.text: `ALTER TABLE sales SET TBLPROPERTIES ('delta.autoClustering' = 'region');` to seed the key selection
`ALTER TABLE sales CLUSTER BY NONE;` then `OPTIMIZE sales ZORDER BY (region);` to let Databricks adapt the z-order
`ALTER TABLE sales CLUSTER BY AUTO (region);` because the column list is an argument of the auto keyword
`ALTER TABLE sales CLUSTER BY (region);` then `ALTER TABLE sales CLUSTER BY AUTO;`

stem: The table `sales_agg` has `CLUSTER BY AUTO` and used to skip well. After a refactor, a nightly job runs `CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE sales_agg AS SELECT ...` without a clustering clause, and filter performance on the table falls back to full scans. The previous clustering columns are also gone. What happened and how is it fixed?

choices.text: Replacing the table without `CLUSTER BY AUTO` turns off automatic clustering and drops the columns, so restate the clause
The nightly job exhausted the key budget of predictive optimization, so its clustering is paused until the next billing month starts
Automatic clustering is disabled for tables created with CTAS, so the table must be created empty and then loaded with `INSERT`
`CREATE OR REPLACE` keeps all clustering properties, so the scans come from stale statistics and need a manual `ANALYZE` on the table

stem: A managed table receives hourly `MERGE` upserts that touch scattered rows, and analysts run selective dashboard queries filtering on `customer_id` and `order_date`. Query and merge times are both poor. A colleague says deletion vectors and Liquid Clustering are alternatives, so only one is needed. What is the best response?

choices.text: Use only deletion vectors, because marking rows in metadata also sorts files by `customer_id` and improves data skipping for the filters
Use both, because deletion vectors reduce file rewrites during the merge while clustering keys improve data skipping for the dashboard filters
Use only clustering, because clustering keys stop `MERGE` from rewriting files by routing updates into the same few files
Use neither, because the table should be partitioned on `customer_id`, which removes both problems at once

stem: A managed events table is queried with filters on `event_date` in nearly every query and on `device_id`, a very high-cardinality column, only in some queries. The engineer wants better skipping on both and wants the low-cardinality column prioritized. Which configuration fits?

choices.text: Cluster by `device_id` only, because a second key always reduces skipping on tables of every size
Cluster by both columns with `event_date` as hierarchical clustering column, and keep `device_id` as a standard key
Partition by `device_id` and cluster by `event_date`, because liquid clustering keys must differ from partition columns
Cluster by both columns and make `device_id` the first hierarchical column, because high-cardinality columns give the strongest prioritization

stem: A wide Delta table has 150 columns. A team clusters it by `CLUSTER BY (merchant_ref)`, where `merchant_ref` is the 70th column, but queries filtering on it still scan nearly every file. Data was recently added by many writers. What is the most likely cause and fix?

choices.text: Liquid clustering supports only string keys of a fixed length, so the column must be cast to a short string before the table is clustered
The table needs partitioning first, because liquid clustering works only on columns that also appear as partition columns
Clustering keys need collected statistics and by default only the first 32 columns have them, so include the column in the statistics columns
Clustering is applied to the first 32 columns only, so the column must be renamed with a prefix that sorts it to the start of the schema

stem: Analysts run dozens of dashboard queries each hour against the same Delta tables on a classic cluster. Reads from cloud storage dominate latency. The engineer suggests adding `df.cache()` calls to every notebook. What is the better approach?

choices.text: Rely on the disk cache on worker types with local SSD, which copies Parquet and Delta files after the first read and needs no code changes
Run `CACHE SELECT` after each write on a SQL warehouse, because the command is the only way to fill the disk cache on warehouses
Add `df.cache()` everywhere, because the disk cache is only available for DataFrames that were explicitly persisted in memory
Set `spark.databricks.io.cache.maxDiskUsage` to zero, because disabling local storage forces faster reads directly from object storage

stem: A team schedules a job after every `MERGE` and `OPTIMIZE` that tries to invalidate the disk cache on all workers, fearing that analysts could read stale rows from cached copies of rewritten files. The job is flaky and adds minutes to each run. What should the engineer conclude?

choices.text: The job is necessary, because the disk cache never detects changes and keeps serving old files until the cluster is restarted
The job is necessary only for streaming reads, because the disk cache serves batch reads from storage metadata but streaming reads from stale copies
The job is necessary only for `OPTIMIZE`, because compaction rewrites files without informing the disk cache although merges do
The job is unnecessary, because the disk cache detects created, deleted, modified and overwritten files and evicts stale entries automatically

stem: A notebook reads a large Delta table, applies a heavy join and aggregation, and then uses the resulting DataFrame in five separate actions. The cluster has SSD workers with the disk cache enabled, but the join still repeats five times. Which technique reduces the repeated work?

choices.text: Increase the disk cache size, because it stores the joined results automatically once it has enough space on the local disk
Run `OPTIMIZE ZORDER` on the source table, because it materializes the join output in the table's layout
Persist the joined DataFrame with the Apache Spark cache, because the disk cache stores source file copies and not transformation results
Rely on the disk cache alone, because it evaluates the lineage of the DataFrame and caches the join result after the first action

stem: A heavily reused DataFrame is persisted with `df.cache()` on an autoscaling cluster. During quiet periods the cluster scales down, and the next report is slower than the first although the data did not change. What is the cause, and what do the docs recommend for repeated reads of Parquet and Delta data?

choices.text: The Spark cache expires after a fixed number of minutes, so a scheduled job must call `cache()` again each hour
The disk cache and the Spark cache share one memory pool, so scaling down halves the pool and evicts the DataFrame
Autoscaling invalidates the Parquet files on storage, so the data must be rewritten with `OPTIMIZE` before the cache can be used again
Removing a worker loses the Spark cache blocks on it and partitions are reread; use the disk cache on SSD workers for repeated file reads

stem: A data engineer created a cluster with worker types that have only network-attached storage. Repeated queries against the same tables are no faster the second time. Which change addresses this with the least configuration?

choices.text: Choose cache-accelerated worker types with local SSD storage, which Databricks configures automatically for the disk cache
Move to a driver-only cluster, because the driver's memory is the only location where the disk cache stores file copies
Add `CACHE SELECT` statements to the notebook, because the command creates SSD volumes for each table it caches
Keep the workers and set `spark.databricks.io.cache.enabled` to true, because the flag alone creates local cache storage on network-only nodes

stem: A team moves a notebook workload to a SQL warehouse. Its warm-up step `CACHE SELECT * FROM sales` appears to do nothing, and the engineer asks whether warm-up is broken. What is the correct statement?

choices.text: The command fails silently because Unity Catalog tables cannot be cached, so the data must be copied to a table in the legacy metastore
The command is ignored on SQL warehouses, which use an enhanced disk caching algorithm automatically, so no manual warm-up is needed
The command needs the Photon engine disabled, so the warehouse must be switched to classic mode before warming
The command works only on clusters with driver memory above a threshold, so the warehouse must be resized to run it

stem: An engineer benchmarks a query for a release and wants to measure cold reads that do not benefit from or populate the disk cache, without deleting anything from the workers. Which setting achieves that?

choices.text: Set `spark.databricks.io.cache.maxMetaDataCache` to zero, which turns off data caching but keeps metadata caching
Set `spark.databricks.io.cache.enabled` to false, which also deletes the files already stored in the local storage of each worker
Set `spark.databricks.io.cache.enabled` to false, which stops queries from reading the cache and from adding new data to it
Set `spark.databricks.io.cache.compression.enabled` to false, which bypasses cached data for every following query

stem: A managed Delta table with row tracking enabled is the target of heavy `MERGE` and `UPDATE` jobs. Legacy change data feed is enabled on it with `delta.enableChangeDataFeed`, which adds write overhead and storage, and downstream jobs read changes through `readChangeFeed`. The platform supports automatic change data feed. What is the correct way to move?

choices.text: Keep legacy change data feed enabled and also enable automatic change data feed, because the two feeds merge into a single change stream
Drop and recreate the table with deletion vectors, because automatic change data feed is implemented as an extension of deletion vectors
Rewrite all downstream readers to use a new `table_changes_auto()` function, because the reading APIs differ between the two approaches
Unset the legacy table property and keep the same `readChangeFeed` and `table_changes()` reads, because both feeds cannot be active together

stem: A downstream job streams the change feed of `silver_orders` with `readChangeFeed` into `gold_orders`. Its checkpoint is corrupted. `gold_orders` already contains all changes up to and including table version 75 of the source, and source versions 70 and above are still in the history. A restart with a new checkpoint and no other option would reload the whole source as inserts. What is the right recovery?

choices.text: Start a new stream with a new checkpoint location and `startingVersion` set to 76, because the target already reflects everything up to 75
Delete the source table history up to version 75 with `VACUUM`, because a stream then starts at the first remaining version
Reuse the corrupted checkpoint with `startingVersion` set to 70, because the checkpoint resumes from the earlier of the two positions
Start with a new checkpoint and `startingVersion` set to 0, because reading change data always requires the first version of the table

stem: A downstream job reads `table_changes('customers', 41, 45)` and applies each row to a dimension table with `MERGE`. Several customers appear more than once in the range, with `update_preimage` and `update_postimage` rows. The merge fails with a multiple-match error on `customer_id`. Which transformation before the merge is correct?

choices.text: Keep all rows and sort by `_commit_timestamp`, because MERGE applies duplicates in the order of the sort column
Drop `update_preimage` rows, keep the highest `_commit_version` row per `customer_id`, and apply deletes from `_change_type = 'delete'`
Group by `_change_type` and take the maximum, because the feed does not contain version information per row
Keep only `update_preimage` rows, because they contain the values that the dimension table must hold after the change

stem: A batch job reads `table_changes('accounts', 10, 30)` on a table with column mapping enabled. Version 22 renamed a column. The job fails, and reading versions 10-21 and 23-30 separately works. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: A query cannot span a non-additive schema change such as a rename, so split the range into parts before and after the change
The job fails because the range exceeds 20 versions, so each read must cover at most 20 versions
Renaming a column permanently disables the feed, so it must be turned on again with a new table property
Change data feed supports only the latest schema, so the job must read from version 22 onward after dropping history before it
